I think maybe it would just be easier if I didn't wake up. If I just stayed asleep forever, you know? It's not that I want to, like, do something drastic. Guilty? Well... I mean, not really, no. I don't think so. It's not like I'm sitting around beating myself up over things I did or didn't do, you know? It's more just... this heavy feeling. I just feel incredibly tired and empty. I mean, sure, I feel bad that I haven't been as present for my wife, and I know I've been a drag to be around. Like last week, she made this really nice pot roast, her mother's recipe, the one she usually only makes for my birthday or our anniversary, and she just made it on a random Tuesday to try and cheer me up. And I sat there at the table, just pushing the carrots around my plate, and I could see the disappointment in her eyes. But even then, it wasn't like a crushing, overwhelming guilt where I was blaming myself for ruining the night. It was more just a dull realization of, "Oh, look, another thing I can't enjoy, another way I'm letting her down." But it's almost like I'm too tired to even muster up a strong feeling of guilt. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I'm blaming myself for things. I'm just sort of existing right now, just floating through the days, waiting for this fog to lift. It's not about feeling bad about the past, it's just about not being able to handle the present.

Anxious? On edge? Well, I mean... no, not really. Not like you'd think. It's funny you ask that, because my brother-in-law, Dave—he's the one married to my sister, Sarah—he's got anxiety. Like, real bad. Can't even go to the grocery store sometimes without feeling like his chest is caving in, sweating through his shirt, the whole nine yards. He's always talking about feeling "on edge," like he's waiting for the other shoe to drop, you know? But for me, it's... it's not like that at all. 

I don't have that nervous energy, that feeling like I need to jump out of my skin or like something terrible is about to happen. If anything, it's the exact opposite. I'm just... flat. Heavy. Like I was saying about the fishing and the records, I don't have the energy to be anxious. Being anxious takes work, you know? Your heart has to beat fast, your brain has to spin a million miles an hour thinking about all the things that could go wrong. My brain just... isn't doing that. It's barely doing anything at all. 

I mean, sure, I guess I get a little stressed at work sometimes, like when the delivery truck is late and we've got contractors waiting on lumber, but that's just normal hardware store stuff. That's not being "on edge." That's just annoyance. Right now, in this whole... funk I'm in, I don't feel nervous. I don't feel panicky. I just feel like I'm moving through molasses. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious. I'm too tired to be anxious, honestly.

Weight? Yeah, I suppose I have. I mean, I haven't exactly been stepping on the scale every morning to chart it or anything, but... yeah, my clothes are definitely fitting differently. Take these jeans I'm wearing right now, for example. These are my standard work jeans, the ones I've worn to the hardware store for the last, I don't know, two years? I look at it, and it just looks like a mountain of work. It looks like too much trouble to even pick up the fork. Moving or speaking slower? Hmm... no, I don't think so. I mean, I know I said I feel like I'm moving through molasses, but that's more about the energy it takes to get up and do things, not the actual speed of it once I'm doing it, if that makes sense. I'm walking at my normal pace, it just feels like my legs weigh a hundred pounds each while I'm doing it. 

And as for talking... well, you can probably tell I don't have much trouble talking. My wife always jokes that I can talk the ear off a brass monkey, and I guess even when I'm feeling this down, I still tend to ramble on a bit. I'm not pausing for long times between words, or slurring, or taking forever to get a sentence out. It's just the normal way I talk, maybe just without the usual enthusiasm. Like, usually I'd be chatting up the regulars at the store, asking about their weekend projects, really getting into it. Now, I'm just giving them the information they need, but I'm saying it at a normal speed. 

I guess I've seen people who get depressed and they just sort of... shut down. They talk real quiet and slow, like every word is a huge effort, and they barely move their hands when they talk. But for me, it's not the physical act of moving or speaking that's slowed down. It's the motivation behind it. It's the spark. The engine is still running at the same RPM, there's just no gas in the tank, you know? So, physically, no, I wouldn't say I'm moving or talking any slower than I usually do. Just feeling heavier while I do it.

I'd come home from a long shift at the hardware store, head straight down to the basement, and just tinker. It was my wind-down time. But now? I look at the fermenter and it just feels like a chore. Same with the records. I'd normally get a real kick out of finding an original pressing, cleaning the dust off, dropping the needle, maybe reading the liner notes while the music plays... but lately, I look at the crates and just think about how much effort it takes to even pick one out and put it on the turntable. \n\nIt's like my brain can't even remember what it feels like to enjoy them. I don't mean to beat a dead horse here, but it's just... everything feels like work now. I know I should have cleaned them back in September, and yeah, my wife got a little annoyed when it rained and the water spilled over the side of the porch, but I don't feel *guilty* about it in the sense that I'm, like, agonizing over it or thinking I'm a terrible person. It's just a fact. Fidgeting? No, not really. I mean, like I was saying before about the molasses feeling, it's not that I'm stuck in place physically. I can move, I can get up and go to the bathroom or go to work. I'm not sitting in a chair for ten hours straight unable to blink, you know? It's more of a mental block. It's the getting started that's the hurdle.

Your heart has to beat fast, your brain has to spin a million miles an hour thinking about all the things that could go wrong. My brain just... isn't doing that. It's barely doing anything at all. \n\nI mean, sure, I guess I get a little stressed at work sometimes, like when the delivery truck is late and we've got contractors waiting on lumber, but that's just normal hardware store stuff. That's not being \"on edge.\" That's just annoyance. Right now, in this whole... funk I'm in, I don't feel nervous. I don't feel panicky. I just feel like I'm moving through molasses. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious. I'm too tired to be anxious, honestly.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?\n\nPatient: Weight? Yeah, I suppose I have. Usually, they fit just fine, maybe even a little snug around the waist after the holidays, you know how that goes. It's just another thing I have to force myself to do, and honestly, half the time, I just don't have the energy to do it. So, yeah, the weight is definitely dropping off, just because I can't be bothered to put the calories in.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that you're moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?\n\nPatient: Moving or speaking slower? Hmm... no, I don't think so. My wife always jokes that I can talk the ear off a brass monkey, and I guess even when I'm feeling this down, I still tend to ramble on a bit. I'm not pausing for long times between words, or slurring, or taking forever to get a sentence out. It's just the normal way I talk, maybe just without the usual enthusiasm. Well, let me think... if I had to put an exact number on it, I’d say this low spell has been hanging on for about three months now. Yeah, right around three months since that crash.

I'd normally get a real kick out of finding an original pressing, cleaning the dust off, dropping the needle, maybe reading the liner notes while the music plays... but lately, I look at the crates and just think about how much effort it takes to even pick one out and put it on the turntable. \n\nIt's like my brain can't even remember what it feels like to enjoy them. I don't mean to beat a dead horse here, but it's just... everything feels like work now. It's not just that I don't want to do them, it's that doing them feels exactly like having to clean the gutters or take out the trash. No, not really. I mean, like I was saying before about the molasses feeling, it's not that I'm stuck in place physically. I can move, I can get up and go to the bathroom or go to work. I'm not sitting in a chair for ten hours straight unable to blink, you know? It's more of a mental block. It's the getting started that's the hurdle. \n\nBut as far as being restless, pacing the floors, wringing my hands, tapping my foot... no, I don't have any of that going on right now. I just sit there. Sometimes I'll sit on the edge of the bed for twenty minutes just looking at my shoes, trying to convince myself to put them on. My wife will come in and ask what I'm doing, and I just tell her I'm getting ready, but really, I'm just sitting. Not bouncing my leg, not picking at my fingernails, just... existing, I guess. \n\nNow, when I was in that other state, back when Mr. Henderson was talking to me through the ceiling, oh boy, that was a different story. I couldn't sit still to save my life. I was pacing the kitchen, rearranging the pantry alphabetically, taking apart the toaster to clean the crumbs out of the coils. I was a ball of nervous energy. But right now? No. I'm just heavy. I don't have the energy to be restless. It takes too much effort to fidget, honestly. I'd rather just sit still and conserve whatever little bit of battery power I have left for the day. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm restless or stuck, just... unmotivated to move unless I absolutely have to.\n\nDoctor: Have you thought about a specific method you would use if you were to act on your thoughts of not wanting to wake up?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was trying to explain earlier, it's not really like that. I haven't thought about a method, because I haven't actually thought about doing anything to myself. It's not a plan. I'm not sitting there trying to figure out the logistics of it, you know? I haven't looked up anything online or thought about what I'd use. I don't own a gun, I don't like guns, never have. And pills... well, my wife keeps all the Tylenol and stuff in the high cabinet anyway, but I wouldn't even know what to take or how much, and frankly, the thought of messing that up and ending up in a hospital bed with a ruined liver or something just sounds worse than what I'm dealing with now. \n\nIt's really just what I said before. It's just this passive thought that floats around in my head when I'm lying there in the dark. It's the reason I finally gave in and came to see you, because my wife kept pushing and pushing, and I realized that having that thought—the one where I just think, \"Man, it would be so much easier if I just didn't wake up tomorrow\"—well, that's probably not a normal thing that healthy people think about on a Tuesday night. \n\nBut there's a big difference, at least in my mind, between wishing you wouldn't wake up and actually taking steps to make sure you don't. I haven't taken any steps. I haven't made any plans. I could never do that to my wife, she'd be the one who'd have to find me, or deal with the aftermath, the funeral, the house, the bills... she doesn't deserve that. She's been nothing but supportive, even when I'm dragging myself around the house like a zombie. So, no, no method. Just the thought. Just the exhaustion of it all making me wish I could hit a pause button that never unpauses. But I haven't plotted anything out, I promise you that.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're unable to initiate or continue activities due to a lack of energy or motivation?\n\nPatient: Unable? Well... no, I wouldn't say unable. That makes it sound like I'm paralyzed or something, and like I was saying before, I'm really not. I can still do things. \n\nI mean, take my job, for instance. I've been at the hardware store for twenty years, and I haven't missed a shift through this whole stretch. Just this past Wednesday, I had the opening shift, which means I have to be there at 6:30 AM to unlock the doors, count the tills, and get the registers ready before the contractors start coming in at seven. Did I want to? No. Did I sit in my car in the parking lot for an extra ten minutes just staring at the steering wheel, listening to the morning radio? Yeah, I did. But I still got out of the car. I still unlocked the doors. \n\nAnd as far as continuing things goes... I don't just stop in the middle of a task. If I start restocking the plumbing aisle—which is my main section, I know every valve and PVC fitting in that place like the back of my hand—I don't just leave a box of pipe elbows sitting on the floor and walk away because I ran out of steam. I finish it. It might take me twice as long as it used to, and I might be dragging my feet the whole time, but I get it done. Same thing at home. My wife asked me to take the trash out the other night, and I didn't just leave the bags halfway down the driveway. I took them all the way to the curb, made sure the lids were on tight so the raccoons wouldn't get in. \n\nSo it's not an inability. It's just... it's like walking through chest-deep water. I'm still participating in life, I'm still helping folks figure out what kind of anchors they need for their drywall, even if it takes absolutely everything in me just to put on my work vest and force a smile. I've always prided myself on being a reliable worker—Mr. Henderson used to always say I was his most dependable guy—so I just push through it. I wouldn't use the word unable at all. I'm just running on fumes, but the engine is still turning over, you know?\n\nDoctor: How many months have you been feeling this way, with no pleasure in activities and feeling heavy, exactly?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think... if I had to put an exact number on it, I’d say this low spell has been hanging on for about three months now. It all felt so pointless. \n\nAnd then Christmas came and went, and it was the exact same story. I didn't even want to put the lights up on the gutters. I did it, eventually, because I always do it and I didn't want the neighbors asking my wife questions, but it took me three days to do what usually takes me a couple of hours on a Saturday afternoon. Ever since that big crash, it's just been one long, gray stretch.
